newsitem.title: FRANCE: French household optimism dips in March.
newsitem.headline: French household optimism dips in March.

text.p: French people gave a dimmer view of the economy and the prospects for living standards and jobs in the latest monthly survey of national household confidence released on Thursday.

The survey carried out in March by the national statistics institute INSEE showed optimism had ebbed slightly compared to the previous month and that families were gloomier about their prospects for living standards and employment.

Economists are cautious about sentiment polls on the grounds that they do not always bear a clear relationship to the way in which consumers actually behave when it comes to spending, and both sets of figures can also prove quite erratic.

The March household sentiment index -- which shows how much negative views outweight positive ones in percentage points -- dipped to minus 32 -- returning to its December level after the improvements of January and February, when it stood at minus 30.
The view of future living standards deteriorated for the second successive month after lifting briefly in December and January.
Feelings on unemployment prospects darkened again after a fillip in February.

Respondents gave a gloomier assessment of their past and future financial situation, but their view of current financial well-being was unchanged from the preceding two months of 1997 and better than in the last months of 1996.

The latest data on actual household spending on manufactured goods showed that it had fallen 1.7 percent in February versus the first month of the year but that this was after a big rise of 3.0 percent in January.

The French government, which needs healthy growth this year to cut its public deficit ahead of European monetary union, is counting on economic growth of at least 2.3 percent this year after 1996 growth in gross domestic product of 1.3 percent.
It is relying on healthy consumer spending to underpin the upturn but also on a pick-up in business investment levels.

Unemployment, currently at a record 12.8 percent, is the big blackspot for the centre-right government and is expected to edge up, but the government and most economists believe it could start to come down again in the second half of 1997.
